title: Job Aids for People Managers & Contract Leads
content: Job Aids for People Managers & Contract Leads These job aids provide practical tools for managing the people and delivery situations that arise on Focus teams. They are intended to help People Managers and Contract Leads respond consistently, distinguish individual concerns from delivery-system problems, and intervene at the appropriate level. Job Aids - Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues — Determine what is preventing a team member from meeting expectations and respond with coaching, performance management, or changes to the delivery system.

title: Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues
content: Job Aid 01: Coaching vs. Performance vs. Systemic Issues When a team member is struggling, the first question should not be “Is this a performance problem?” The first question is: What is preventing this person from consistently meeting the expectation? A missed commitment, communication breakdown, quality concern, or lack of ownership can have very different root causes. Before escalating an issue, determine whether you are dealing with a coaching issue, performance issue, or systemic issue . The Three Categories Category What it means Manager's responsibility --- --- --- Coaching Issue The person needs additional skill, clarity, feedback, experience, or support to consistently meet the expectation. Teach, clarify, demonstrate, provide feedback, and create opportunities to practice. Performance Issue The expectation is reasonable and understood, the person has the capability and support to meet it, but the gap continues despite feedback and coaching. Establish accountability, document the recurring gap, set explicit improvement expectations, and follow Focus's performance-management process when appropriate. Systemic Issue The environment, process, workload, dependencies, leadership decisions, or team structure are preventing reliable performance. Fix the system rather than treating the individual as the problem. The Diagnostic When you observe a delivery concern, work through these questions before categorizing it as a performance issue : Ask If NO... If YES... --- --- --- 1. Is the expectation clear and appropriate for this person's role and level? Clarify the expectation. Continue. 2. Is the person reasonably in control of the outcome? Investigate dependencies/system constraints. Continue. 3. Does the person have the knowledge and skill to meet the expectation? Coach/develop. Continue. 4. Has the person received specific feedback about the gap? Give feedback. Continue. 5. Have reasonable support, resources, and time been provided? Provide support. Continue. 6. Does the same gap continue after expectations, feedback, and support are clear? Continue coaching/observation. This may now be a performance issue . A useful shorthand is: CAN'T → Coaching The person does not yet have the skill, experience, clarity, or judgment needed to consistently meet the expectation. WON'T / ISN'T → Performance The person understands the expectation, has the capability and reasonable support to meet it, has received feedback, and the behavior or outcome continues. CAN'T BECAUSE → Systemic Something in the team's environment is preventing success. Evidence Before Labels Retro comments, stakeholder feedback, missed sprint commitments, defects, escalations, or concerns raised by another lead should be treated as signals , not conclusions. Before having a performance conversation, the manager should be able to answer: 1. What specifically happened? 2. What was expected instead? 3. Was that expectation previously clear? 4. What impact did the gap have? 5. What feedback or coaching has already been provided? 6. Has the behavior occurred repeatedly? Avoid labels such as: “You aren't taking ownership.” Instead, describe observable behavior and the expected behavior: “On the last two deliverables, I had to follow up several times to understand status and next steps. At your level, I expect you to proactively communicate progress, surface blockers, and close the loop without repeated prompting.” Specific behavior can be coached. Vague character judgments cannot. Common Scenarios Scenario Start Here What to investigate --- --- --- Team member requires repeated follow-ups Coaching Do they understand expectations for follow-through, prioritization, and closing loops? Progress isn't visible to the team or lead Coaching / Systemic Is work actually stalled, or is progress simply not being communicated? Senior team member isn't demonstrating expected ownership Coaching / Role Clarity Have ownership expectations for their level been explicitly established? Decisions are difficult to understand or poorly explained Coaching Can they clearly communicate the recommendation, rationale, tradeoffs, and next action? Team member repeatedly surfaces problems without helping move them forward Coaching Do they know when they are expected to recommend an action, facilitate resolution, or escalate? Team member reports that work is on track, declines support, then repeatedly misses commitments Potential Performance Issue Were risks knowable, expectations clear, and support available? Is this recurring after feedback? Several team members are struggling with the same issue Systemic Look at workload, priorities, dependencies, process, leadership, tooling, and role clarity. Individual has too many competing priorities Systemic first Who established the priorities? What should be stopped or deprioritized? Team receives conflicting direction from leaders Systemic Leadership must align priorities and decision rights before evaluating individual execution. Team member struggles with a new responsibility they've never performed before Coaching Determine what training, modeling, pairing, or feedback they need. A Missed Commitment Is Not Automatically a Performance Issue In delivery environments, commitments move. Requirements change. Dependencies fail. Stakeholders introduce new priorities. Technical complexity emerges. The manager should therefore investigate how the individual managed the commitment , not merely whether the date was missed. There is a meaningful difference between: “We're at risk of missing Friday because the dependency hasn't been resolved. I've escalated it, and here are our options.” and: “Everything is fine.” followed by an unexpected miss. The second situation may indicate a reliability or judgment concern because the team lost the opportunity to manage the risk. Expectations for Senior Team Members and Leads As responsibility increases, Focus expects greater independence in creating clarity and moving work forward. Senior team members should increasingly be able to: - Own the outcome , not simply complete assigned tasks. - Surface risk early , while the team still has options. - Close the loop without repeated prompting. - Make thinking visible by clearly explaining decisions and tradeoffs. - Move problems forward , even when they do not personally know the solution. - Protect team focus by identifying competing priorities and escalating capacity constraints. This does not mean leaders must always arrive with a solution. A healthy escalation can be: “I don't know the solution yet. Here's what I think is happening, here's what I've tried, and here's where I need help.” The expectation is not “Never bring me a problem.” The expectation is “Help move the problem forward.” Moving From Coaching to Performance Management A coaching issue should not remain in an informal coaching loop indefinitely. Consider transitioning into formal performance management when: Expectation is clear → Capability exists → Feedback has been given → Support has been provided → Reasonable time has passed → The same material gap continues At that point, the conversation changes from: Coaching: “Let's work on helping you become more effective at this.” to: Performance: “This is an expectation of your role, we've discussed the gap and provided support, and the required improvement has not occurred consistently.” People Managers should involve the appropriate Focus leadership/People Operations before beginning formal performance action. Scrum Metrics Are Signals, Not Individual Scorecards Do not use velocity, story points completed, ticket counts, PR counts, bugs, or similar Scrum metrics as standalone measures of individual performance. They can help identify where investigation is needed, but they rarely explain why something is happening. Evaluate people more holistically through: Reliability • Quality • Ownership • Collaboration • Judgment • Communication • Role Competency • Impact The goal is not to create a delivery organization where everyone learns how to make their metrics look green. The goal is to create teams where problems become visible early enough to solve them.

title: Job Aid 02: Giving Effective Feedback
content: Job Aid 02: Giving Effective Feedback Why feedback matters and how People Managers and Contract Leads can make it useful. Feedback gives people information they need to succeed: what is working, what needs to change, and how their actions affect others. When a concern stays in a lead's head or circulates among colleagues, the person involved has little opportunity to understand it or respond. This job aid applies principles from Claire Hughes Johnson's Scaling People and Crucial Conversations to Focus delivery situations. The examples and suggested cadence below are practical applications for our teams. Why Giving Feedback Is Part of Leading Leads see things that individual team members may not: the downstream effect of a late handoff, the uncertainty created by a missing update, or the value of a well-timed escalation. Sharing those observations helps people connect their work to team outcomes. - Make expectations visible. Explain what good looks like for the person's role and level. An expectation that has never been communicated needs to be established before someone can fairly be held to it. - Give people time to adjust. Raise concerns while the details are fresh and there is an opportunity to practice a different approach. Waiting for a review or the next retro can allow the same issue to repeat. - Reinforce what works. Specific positive feedback tells people which behaviors to repeat and helps the team learn from good delivery practices. - Improve the manager's understanding. The conversation may reveal unclear priorities, missing support, or a decision the lead needs to revisit. A concern discussed among leads still needs an appropriate conversation with the person involved. Talking about someone does not give them feedback. This supports Focus's existing approach of active coaching and clear expectations. Use Job Aid 01 to distinguish coaching, performance, and systemic concerns as you learn more. Principles from Scaling People Hughes Johnson emphasizes managerial self-awareness, curiosity when coaching, and the willingness to surface difficult topics. She describes feedback as a partnership in which the manager offers observations and explores what is happening, rather than assuming they already have the answer. See her discussion of these principles. Apply that approach by: - Checking your own contribution. Was the expectation clear? Did your direction change? Are you reacting to a work-style preference or a meaningful delivery gap? - Bringing an observation and a question. Be specific about what you saw, then investigate the explanation together. - Naming the concern respectfully. If a recurring issue matters to the work or relationship, make it discussable. Avoid hints that require the other person to guess what you mean. Prepare for a Crucial Conversation Start with Heart: Identify the outcome you want for the person, the team, and your working relationship. Check whether frustration has shifted your goal toward winning an argument or proving someone wrong. Explain your constructive purpose when you open the conversation. Crucial Learning: Start with Heart. Make It Safe: Show respect for the person and concern for shared goals. If the conversation becomes defensive or shuts down, pause to understand what feels threatening and clarify your intent. Give them room to disagree and correct your interpretation while keeping the expectation clear. Crucial Learning: Make It Safe. For sensitive individual feedback, choose a private conversation with enough time to listen. Prepare one or two concrete examples and the impact you can substantiate. Distinguish what you observed directly from what someone else reported, and avoid presenting secondhand concerns as established facts. Use STATE to Open the Dialogue The STATE framework helps you explain your perspective and invite the other person's. The last two skills describe how to speak throughout the conversation. Crucial Learning's explanation of STATE. Skill How to apply it --- --- Share your facts Describe a specific event or behavior that could be observed. Avoid labels such as “unreliable” or “not committed.” Tell your story Explain the concern or interpretation the facts raise for you. Distinguish an actual impact from a risk you anticipate. Ask for others' paths Invite their account of what happened. Listen before choosing a response. Talk tentatively Treat your explanation of the cause as something to examine. You can be certain about an agreed expectation while remaining curious about why it was missed. Encourage testing Explicitly welcome corrections, missing context, and a different interpretation. Change your view when the evidence warrants it. Example: Repeated Follow-Ups “I'd like us to make handoffs easier to plan. On the last two deliverables, the agreed status update wasn't posted, and I asked twice before learning the next steps. That left me unable to confirm the handoff with the team. I'm concerned our current approach isn't making progress and blockers visible enough. What was happening from your perspective? Is there context I'm missing?” Pause and listen. If the update expectation was unclear, clarify it. If competing assignments prevented progress, address the priorities. If a known expectation was missed, discuss what will help the person meet it consistently. Then agree on a concrete next step, for example: “For the next two weeks, please post progress, the next step, and any blocker in the agreed channel before our check-in. I'll clarify which assignment takes priority today. Let's review how this is working at next week's 1:1.” Example: Reinforcing Good Practice “You flagged the dependency risk before planning and brought two options. That gave us time to adjust the commitment with the client. Please keep surfacing risks that early; it helps the team make decisions while we still have options.” Common Scenarios Situation Useful response --- --- A concern appears in a retro Use the retro to understand the team pattern. Follow up privately on individual behavior; do not turn the group discussion into an individual performance review. You are waiting for the person to notice the problem State the observation, impact, and expectation directly. Seniority does not make unspoken expectations clear. The person disagrees or becomes upset Listen for missing facts or a misunderstanding. A reaction alone does not establish a performance issue. If needed, agree on a short pause and a specific time to resume. The same gap continues after feedback Revisit the agreed action and support, then use Job Aid 01 to assess what remains unresolved. Involve the People Manager and appropriate Focus leadership/People Operations before formal performance action. Someone gives you difficult feedback Ask for an example, check your understanding, and explain what you will do with the input. Follow up on your own commitments. For issues covered by Focus's Conduct & Ethics or Incident Response procedures, use the applicable reporting path; this job aid does not add a requirement to confront someone first. End with Action and Follow Through Crucial Conversations emphasizes turning dialogue into specific commitments: identify an owner, the action, a deadline, and a follow-up. A conversation can feel productive while leaving those decisions unresolved. Al Switzler on moving to action. Before closing, confirm: - The behavior to continue or change and what success will look like. - The support or system change the lead will provide. - Who is responsible for each action and when it will happen. - When you will review progress together. Keep a brief factual recap in the appropriate private working notes or management record. Include the person's perspective and the lead's commitments. Recognize improvement at follow-up and address any remaining gap explicitly. Suggested Practice Before the Next Retro Use the next 30 days as a learning window, adjusting timing to the situation: 1. Early in the window: Choose one meaningful concern, gather examples, and have the conversation. Also identify a helpful behavior to reinforce. 2. During the window: Check progress at an agreed 1:1. Complete your own support commitments and adjust the approach if new information changes the diagnosis. 3. At the next retro: Discuss team-level actions, what changed, and what remains blocked. Keep individual feedback and personnel details in the appropriate private conversations. The next retro is a checkpoint. Give feedback when it can help, rather than saving it for that meeting.
